lessons.title: SQL Basics: SELECT & Aggregation
lessons.goal: Pull rows from a table and collapse them into per-group summaries, like total revenue per sales rep.

example.code:
SELECT rep_name, SUM(revenue) AS total
FROM sales
GROUP BY rep_name
ORDER BY total DESC
LIMIT 1;

keyConcepts: Any column in **SELECT** that isn't wrapped in an aggregate function (SUM, COUNT, AVG) must appear in **GROUP BY** — the database needs to know how to collapse the other rows.
**ORDER BY ... DESC** sorts groups from highest to lowest based on the aggregate value.
**LIMIT 1** keeps only the top row after sorting — that's how you isolate a single 'winner'.

syntaxTemplate.code:
SELECT <group_column>, <AGG_FUNC>(<value_column>) AS <alias>
FROM <table>
GROUP BY <group_column>
ORDER BY <alias> DESC
LIMIT 1;

lessons.proTip: If you SELECT a raw column that isn't aggregated and isn't in GROUP BY, most databases will error out (or silently pick an arbitrary row) — double-check every non-aggregated column is listed.

lessons.title: SQL Joins: Combining Tables
lessons.goal: Combine rows from two related tables, and optionally find rows that exist in one table but not the other.

example.code:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

keyConcepts: **INNER JOIN** only keeps rows that match in both tables; **LEFT JOIN** keeps every row from the left table even without a match, filling unmatched columns with NULL.
To find 'things with no match' (e.g. customers with zero orders), LEFT JOIN then filter **WHERE right_column IS NULL**.
Window functions like `SUM(...) OVER (ORDER BY ...)` compute running totals without collapsing rows the way GROUP BY does.

syntaxTemplate.code:
SELECT <left>.<col>
FROM <left_table> <left>
LEFT JOIN <right_table> <right> ON <left>.<key> = <right>.<key>
WHERE <right>.<col> IS NULL;

lessons.proTip: Forgetting IS NULL after a LEFT JOIN is the #1 mistake — without it you just get every row, matched or not, and lose the 'missing rows' filter entirely.

lessons.title: Pandas: Cleaning & Normalizing Data
lessons.goal: Rescale a numeric column into a consistent 0-1 range so it plays nicely with ML models that are sensitive to feature scale.
keyConcepts: Min-max normalization maps the smallest value to 0 and the largest to 1, preserving relative spacing between values.
You must compute **min()** and **max()** from the same column you're transforming — mixing columns breaks the scale.
This differs from standardization (z-score), which centers data around a mean of 0 instead of a fixed 0-1 range.
lessons.proTip: If max() and min() are equal (a constant column), this formula divides by zero — guard against that edge case before normalizing.

lessons.title: Pandas: Handling Missing Data
lessons.goal: Detect and fill missing values in a dataframe before running any analysis on it.
keyConcepts: **isna()** returns a True/False mask for missing values; chaining **.sum()** counts how many are missing.
**fillna()** fills gaps with a value you choose — the column mean is a common, simple default for numeric data.
**dropna()** is the alternative — it removes rows/columns with gaps entirely, costing you data instead of estimating it.
lessons.proTip: Filling with the mean can distort skewed data (like income) — median is often the safer default when outliers are present.

lessons.title: scikit-learn: Fitting a Classifier
lessons.goal: Train a model to predict a target column, like churn, from a set of feature columns.

example.code:
model = RandomForestClassifier()
model.fit(X, y)
predictions = model.predict(X)

keyConcepts: **X** is your feature matrix (input columns); **y** is your target column (what you're predicting).
**.fit(X, y)** trains the model by learning patterns that connect features to the target.
**.predict(new_X)** applies what the model learned to new, unseen rows.
lessons.proTip: Fitting and predicting on the exact same data (like the quick example above) hides overfitting — always split into train/test sets in real projects.

lessons.title: Password Hashing Basics
lessons.goal: Convert a plaintext password into a hash so the raw password is never stored anywhere.
keyConcepts: Hashing is one-way — you can't reverse a hash back into the original password, only compare a new hash against the stored one.
**.encode()** converts the string into bytes, which hashlib requires as input.
**.hexdigest()** returns the hash as a readable hex string, ready to store in a database.
lessons.proTip: SHA-256 alone is fast — too fast for password storage in production, since attackers can brute-force it quickly. Real systems add a per-user salt and a slow algorithm like bcrypt or Argon2.

lessons.title: Log Analysis: Spotting Brute Force
lessons.goal: Scan a list of login attempts and flag IPs with an unusually high number of failures.

example.code:
from collections import Counter
failed = Counter(ip for ip, status in logs if status == 'FAILED')
flagged = [ip for ip, c in failed.items() if c > 5]

keyConcepts: **Counter** tallies how many times each unique value (here, each IP) appears in an iterable.
A conditional comprehension (`if status == 'FAILED'`) filters before counting, so only failures get tallied.
The threshold (`c > 5`) turns raw counts into an actionable alert list — tune it based on what's normal for your traffic.

syntaxTemplate.code:
counts = Counter(<key> for <item> in <data> if <condition>)
flagged = [k for k, c in counts.items() if c > <threshold>]

lessons.proTip: A fixed threshold like 5 ignores time — 5 failures in 1 minute is very different from 5 failures over a month. Real systems usually bucket by a time window too.

lessons.title: Preventing SQL Injection
lessons.goal: Rewrite a query built from raw string concatenation so user input can't be used to inject arbitrary SQL.
keyConcepts: String-concatenating user input directly into SQL text lets an attacker close your quote early and inject their own SQL.
Parameterized queries use a placeholder (`?` or `%s`) and pass values separately — the driver escapes them safely.
This matters even if the input 'looks safe' in casual testing; injection payloads are specifically designed to slip past shallow checks.
lessons.proTip: Never assume 'we sanitize on the frontend' is enough — always parameterize on the backend, since frontend checks can be bypassed entirely.

lessons.title: Error Handling: try/except
lessons.goal: Catch a failure so it's logged and visible, instead of crashing silently or crashing the whole program.
keyConcepts: **try** wraps the risky code; **except** catches errors raised inside it instead of letting them crash the program.
An empty except block (`except: pass`) is worse than no try/except at all — it hides failures completely.
Logging the exception (`log.error(e)`) preserves the failure reason so you can debug it later, even though execution continues.
lessons.proTip: Catching the broad `Exception` is fine as a top-level safety net, but catching specific exception types closer to the error gives you more useful handling.

lessons.title: Refactoring: Don't Repeat Yourself
lessons.goal: Extract logic that's copy-pasted in multiple places into a single, reusable function.
keyConcepts: If you find yourself copy-pasting the same block in three places, that's a signal to extract it into a function.
A reusable function centralizes behavior — fix a bug once, and every call site benefits automatically.
Good function names describe **what** the function does, not **how** it does it (e.g. `fetch_data`, not `get_stuff_from_url_and_parse`).
lessons.proTip: Extracting too early — before you have 2-3 real duplicates — can add unnecessary abstraction. 'Rule of three' is a decent gut check.
